title: Hellenistic kingdoms (Seleucid, Ptolemaic, Antigonid)
summary: When Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE, his generals, the Diadochi, met at Babylon, then fought a series of wars over his empire. By 300 BCE it had split into three large parts, and after 280 BCE three great states remained: Antigonid Macedonia, Ptolemaic Egypt and the Seleucid kingdom in Asia. Centralised kingdoms replaced the city-state model, and Greek rule and new colonies spread Hellenic culture across these lands. Weakened by constant wars, they fell to rivals and to Rome, which took Egypt, the last, in 31 BCE.

uncertainty.note: Begins with Alexander’s death in 323 BCE; WHE ends the period with Rome’s conquest of Egypt in 31 BCE.

importance.justification: Spread Greek rule and culture from Egypt to Asia for three centuries before Rome (R3 D3 T3 L3).

related.because: Alexander's unexpected death without an adult heir left his vast empire to be partitioned by his rival generals into separate dynasties.
